variants.name: Classic CRTP with static_cast downcast
variants.idiom_name: class template parameterized on the derived type + static_cast<Derived*>(this)
variants.implementation_notes: The classic form: struct D : Base<D>, with Base::interface() reaching the hook through static_cast<Derived*>(this); the bodies of the base's member functions are instantiated only after D is complete, which is what makes the downcast legal, and every call is resolved statically. Use it for mixins (Barton-Nackman operator suites), per-type static counters, clone(), and facade skeletons, and keep the base parameterized on nothing but the derived type so the CRTP argument stays unambiguous.
pitfalls: Two classes deriving from the same specialization compile and then invoke undefined behaviour inside the base's static_cast; prevent it with a private base constructor plus friendship, or a static_assert / derived_from constraint.
Base and derived members with the same name hide each other (nothing is virtual, no override checking): an accidental shadow is legal code and silently wins.
The base must not be usable as a standalone type - it may cast this to a type that is not there, so its constructors belong in protected or private.

variants.name: CRTP with C++20 concept constraints
variants.idiom_name: requires std::derived_from<Derived, Base<Derived>> on the base and its clients
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 concepts put the CRTP contract where the compiler can report it: constrain client overloads (and, if written carefully, the base) with requires std::derived_from<Derived, Base<Derived>> so a wrong type argument fails at the point of use instead of deep inside the base body, and so generic algorithms can be overloaded for any CRTP-derived type. The mechanism is unchanged - same cast, same static resolution, same cost - but diagnostics and overload sets improve; the price is a C++20 toolchain for every translation unit that includes the header.
pitfalls: Constraints document and diagnose but do not remove the cast: the static_cast inside the base is still unchecked, so the private-constructor or static_assert guard remains necessary.
A loose constraint moves the error to the constraint instead of the mistake; constrain on the exact base instantiation, not on the derived type alone.
Requiring C++20 for a header is a toolchain decision that propagates to every consumer.

variants.name: Deducing this (C++23 explicit object parameter)
variants.idiom_name: template <class Self> void f(this Self&& self)
variants.implementation_notes: C++23 explicit object parameters make the object parameter explicit and deduce it to the derived type, so the base stops being a template: struct Base { template <class Self> void interface(this Self&& self) { self.impl(); } };. No template argument, no cast and no recurrence are needed, which also removes the complexity that piles up with multi-level CRTP. The standard paper (P0847) states the restriction that keeps classic CRTP alive: an explicit object member function cannot be static or virtual, so hooks that must reach static members or nested types of the derived class still use the classic form.
pitfalls: Explicit object member functions cannot be static or virtual, and this is not usable inside them: all member access goes through the named self parameter.
Compiler support is still uneven; keep the classic form or a feature-test macro (__cpp_explicit_this_parameter) as the fallback for older toolchains.
It deduces the static type at the call site, so it is still static polymorphism: behaviour through a base reference does not become polymorphic.
